tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

# Capture — agent notes

## What this is

Single-purpose macOS overlay launcher for Charles's Bear-based second brain. Press a global hotkey, a flat themed bar opens, type a thought, hit Enter — then a destination picker filters projects/people/personal areas as you type. Enter on the pinned Inbox row (or with nothing typed) sends the capture to the pinned Bear "Inbox" note; Enter on a destination files it **immediately**, verbatim, into that note. A second hotkey opens Process Inbox: Tinder-style triage of existing inbox items.

The point is **speed**: hotkey → bar → Enter → gone. Lives entirely as a menu-bar app. No history, no plugins, no main window, no Dock icon. The bar persists when focus is lost — only Esc / Enter / the hotkey itself hide it. Multi-line capture grows the bar downward up to 5 lines, then scrolls internally.

## Design principles (Charles's explicit choices — don't violate)

1. **Speed is the product.** Every keystroke-to-paint under 300ms; in practice <1ms because the keystroke path never does I/O. Destinations live in memory (refreshed async at launch, on every panel show, and via the Refresh Projects menu item). All Bear writes are optimistic: the panel hides / triage advances instantly, work happens behind it.
2. **bearcli for everything.** All Bear I/O goes through the `BearCLI` actor wrapping `/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli` (ships inside Bear 2.8+, works headless). Writes only via CAS: `cat --format json` (returns `content` + `hash`) → transform → `overwrite --base <hash>`; a concurrent Bear.app change rejects the write (exit 1, "Note has changed since last read") and we re-read and retry ×3. **A whole-note `cat` is the only source of the hash.** It used to be `show --fields hash,content`; bearcli 2.9.x dropped `hash` from `show`'s field set, which broke every read with "Unknown field: hash" — triage closed instantly and captures silently took the fallback path (2026-08-23). Re-check this if bearcli is upgraded. **Never write Bear's SQLite directly.** The x-callback URI template survives only as the fallback path.
3. **No daemons, no background agents.** No queues, no Redis, no background workers, no launchd. Charles explicitly rejected daemon infra — don't reintroduce it. The per-capture `claude -p` filing agent was removed on 2026-10-13: the second brain's rule is that nothing writes to Bear in the background.
4. **A capture is never lost.** Every failure path degrades to an Inbox write via the fallback URI template with a backtick-wrapped `` → `#tag` `` marker (backticks so Bear doesn't tag the Inbox note) plus a notification. The triage parser skips marker-carrying blocks.
5. **Human decides, verbatim lands.** The picker is Charles's routing decision. A capture lands exactly as typed and stays where it lands; turning captures into notes is his job.
6. **Themed minimal UI, modelled on [Gyors](https://github.com/balintb/Gyors)** (2026-08 restyle; its macOS layer is SwiftUI over an `NSPanel`, so its numbers port directly). **Ember default** — Gyors' published theme, verbatim: bg `#120C10`, accent `#F97316`, text `#FBF3EC`/`#A89B91`/`#6B5E54`, backgroundOpacity 0.88. Eleven themes in Settings (`Theme.swift`, one struct literal each: Ember, Solarized Light/Dark, Gruvbox Light/Dark, Catppuccin Latte/Mocha, Nord, Dracula, Tokyo Night, Mono Dark).
   - **Three text tiers**: `foreground` (primary) / `secondary` (banner, status — real content) / `dim` (hints, placeholders, ms readout). **Never bake `.opacity()` into a text colour** — over the blur substrate the alpha multiplies and the text goes mushy. Use a solid hex. Alpha on `selectionBackground` is fine; it's a background.
   - **Translucency**: `NSVisualEffectView` (`.popover`, `.behindWindow`, `.active`) as a sibling of the hosting view; per-theme `usesBlur` + `backgroundOpacity`. Charles declined Raycast's glass in 2026-07 but chose Gyors' in 2026-08.
   - **Geometry**: 720 wide, cornerRadius 14 (was 16), 20pt gutter everywhere so the leaf name lines up under the typed text, 36pt rows, no border, instant show/hide, no row icons, no footer bar, no `>` prompt glyph.
   - **Type**: SF Pro throughout (Charles found a pixel font "too much"). Both inputs 22pt `.light`; leaf name 14pt `.medium`; banner 13; chip 11 semibold; hints and ms readout 11.
   - **Selection**: flat full-bleed `accent × selectionOpacity` across the whole row, radius 0, no inset (replaced 2026-07's inset rounded highlight).
   - **`Divider().opacity(0.3)`** full-bleed between the query row and the list.
   - **TheyDo chips** right-aligned per row (2026-07, replaced rainbow badges Charles disliked): one shared hue set `Theme.theydoKinds` (violet/pink/teal/amber/blue/ink-gray/orange for lists/grape for agendas), a pastel **gradient** fill + same-hue tinted text via `Theme.chip(for:)`, derived against each theme's background/foreground so chips adapt to light/dark. `kindColors` stays per-theme-overridable (Mono Dark overrides to stay monochrome).
   - Fixed-height 8-row **scrollable** viewport (empty query lists *all* destinations; the panel never resizes while filtering — only on stage transitions).
   - Placeholder text must be explicitly themed via `prompt: Text(...).foregroundColor(theme.secondary)` — default placeholders ignore the theme and vanish on dark themes. `secondary`, not `dim`: `dim` is the tertiary tone and reads too dark for a placeholder (Charles, 2026-08-21).

## Project layout

```
project.yml                 XcodeGen spec — single source of truth for the Xcode project
Sources/
  CaptureApp.swift          @main App + MenuBarExtra (Open/Process Inbox/Refresh) + Settings scene
  AppDelegate.swift         .accessory policy, both hotkeys, panel lifecycle, --show-on-launch dev flag
  LauncherPanel.swift       NSPanel subclass (non-activating, transparent, blur sibling, children clipped)
  LauncherView.swift        Stage-driven SwiftUI view: compose / route / loading / done
  LauncherModel.swift       @Observable stage machine (capture + triage modes, all transitions)
  DestinationListView.swift Fixed-height scrollable viewport, TheyDo chips right-aligned, full-bleed accent selection
  Theme.swift               Eleven Theme structs (Ember default), three text tiers, blur/opacity knobs, chip hues
  BearCLI.swift             actor — Process wrapper for bearcli, CAS casEdit core
  Destination.swift         Destination + Kind + IndexedDestination (precomputed normalization)
  DestinationStore.swift    Merged list across providers, per-provider state + cache, MRU usage
  Destinations/             DestinationProvider protocol; BearProvider; FifteenFive{Provider,Auth}; MCPClient
  DestinationRanker.swift   Pure per-keystroke ranking (prefix > word-boundary > subsequence)
  CaptureRouter.swift       All write orchestration + pure text transforms + routings.jsonl
  InboxParser.swift         Inbox note → [InboxEntry] (oldest-first, marker/tag-line aware)
  Notify.swift              Failure-only UserNotifications
  DailyCapture.swift        FALLBACK x-callback path ({content}/{time}/{date}/{datetime}/{marker})
  HotkeyName.swift          .toggleLauncher (⌃⌘Space) + .triageInbox (⌃⌘⇧Space)
  SettingsView.swift        Theme, hotkeys, one section per destination (Bear, 15Five sign-in), fallback template
Resources/
  AppIcon.icns
scripts/
  dev.sh                    fswatch + xcodegen + xcodebuild Debug + relaunch loop
  release.sh                xcodegen + xcodebuild Release + ditto zip for GitHub Releases
```

The `.xcodeproj` is generated by XcodeGen and gitignored: `xcodegen generate` after editing `project.yml` or adding/removing source files (`scripts/dev.sh` does it on every save).

## Data flow

```
capture:  ⏎ text → picker → ⏎ dest ──BearCLI casEdit──▶ dest note's section (see below)
                          → ⏎ inbox ──BearCLI casEdit──▶ Inbox note (prepend under H1)
triage:   entry prefilled (editable) → picker → ⏎ dest    same, under the entry's ORIGINAL timestamp, + remove block
                                              → ⏎ inbox   keep it in the Inbox and move on (same as ⇥)
                                              → ⌘⌫        remove block only  ·  ⇥ skip  ·  esc exit
any bearcli failure ─▶ DailyCapture.send(text, marker:) → Inbox via x-callback + notification
```

- **Destination providers** (`Sources/Destinations/`). A `DestinationProvider` lists destinations and files a capture; `DestinationStore` merges every enabled provider into one picker list, sorted by recency, and keeps per-provider state and cache (`destinations-<provider>.json`). A failing provider keeps its cached rows. Ids are provider-qualified (`bear:<note id>`, `fifteenFive:<person id>`). Enable flags: UserDefaults `destination.<provider>.enabled` (Bear on, others off by default). The Inbox row and triage mechanics stay in `CaptureRouter`, always Bear. A failed write parks the capture in the Inbox with ` → Title` (Bear) or ` → Title (15Five)`. Adding a destination = a new provider + a case in `ProviderID` + a Settings section.
- **15Five** (`FifteenFiveProvider`). Remote MCP at `https://my.15five.com/mcp`, the only 15Five write path: the public REST API's `/one-on-one/` is GET-only. Needs 15Five MCP **Access** and **Updates** switched on in Agents Hub > Integrations. One row per person from `list_one_on_one_counterparts`, ranked by next meeting date; Enter calls `add_one_on_one_talking_point` (starts an undated 1-on-1 if none is upcoming; the other person sees it). Talking points only, never action items (Charles, 2026-10-14). Called as a plain API with the exact contract read from the live `tools/list` (2026-10-14), no guessing: both tools wrap arguments in `params`. List: `{params: {limit: 100, offset}}`, paging on `has_more`/`next_offset`, rows `user_id`, `name`, `next_meeting_date`. Write: `{params: {with_user_id, description, request_id}}`, success when `receipt.applied` (or `replay` for a retried `request_id`). A changed shape throws `MCPError` naming the tool and the capture parks in the Inbox. Live schemas are logged to `~/Library/Logs/Capture/15five-tools.json` on each refresh for diagnosis only.
  - **Auth**: OAuth discovered at `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`: dynamic registration, auth code + PKCE S256, public client, refresh tokens, scope `mcp:tools`, redirect `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` from a one-shot `NWListener` (`LoopbackCallback`), login opened in the default browser. 15Five rejects custom-scheme redirects (`capture://` → `invalid_redirect_uri`), so `ASWebAuthenticationSession` with a custom scheme can't work; each sign-in registers a client with that exact port. Credentials live in the Keychain (`com.charlesbeaumont.Capture.15five`); `FifteenFiveTokens` serialises refreshes. Unused connections expire after 30 days: sign in again from Settings.
  - **MCP client**: `NativeMCPClient`, a ~150-line Streamable HTTP client (initialize, tools/list, tools/call, JSON or SSE responses, one retry on 401/404) instead of the Swift MCP SDK, to keep one dependency. `MCPToolCaller` is the seam if another transport is ever wanted.
- **Destinations follow the second brain** (`~/Workspace/second-brain/CLAUDE.md`, flattened 2026-10). Tags are flat and the title is the identity: every note tagged `#project`, `#personal`, `#person`, `#list` or `#agenda` is one destination, shown by title. `#archive`, `#unsorted`, `#reference`, `#output`, `#reflection` are never routable. No registry note, no paused state, no nested `project/x` tags; all three are gone.
- **Write contract** (matches the `review-captures` skill): one line `- **YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM**: text`, multi-line bodies indented two spaces. Projects, personal and people: top of `## Captures` (newest first). Lists: bottom of `## Captures`. Agendas: bottom of `## Topics`. A missing section is created above the trailing tag line, or at the end when the tag isn't last. Never write anywhere else in a note.
- **Fallback marker**: a parked capture's header gets ` → <destination title>`, the routing hint `review-captures` reads.
- **Ranking**: title-prefix 100 > word-boundary 80 > fuzzy subsequence 40+compactness, plus recency `20·exp(−ageDays/14)` and MRU `15·exp(−idx/5)` keyed by note id. Empty query = top rows by recency+MRU with Inbox pinned at row 0, so ⏎⏎ means "straight to inbox" (capture) or "keep it there" (triage).
- **Logs**: `~/Library/Logs/Capture/routings.jsonl`, one record per routing decision with the destination title and note id.

## Build / verify

- Full build: `xcodegen generate && xcodebuild -project Capture.xcodeproj -scheme Capture -configuration Debug build`, or ⌘R in Xcode.
- Launch with the panel already open (no hotkey needed): pass `--show-on-launch` or `--triage-on-launch` to the binary.
- Pure logic (transforms, parser, ranker, destination discovery) can be smoke-tested by compiling the non-UI sources with a scratch `main.swift`:
  `swiftc -enable-bare-slash-regex -target arm64-apple-macos26.0 Sources/{Notify,BearCLI,Destination,DestinationStore,DestinationRanker,InboxParser,CaptureRouter,DailyCapture}.swift Sources/Destinations/*.swift /tmp/main.swift -o /tmp/t && /tmp/t`
- Behavior is otherwise verified by running the app against Bear.

## Hard constraints

- **macOS 26 Tahoe only**, Swift 6. Personal tool; no backward-compat fallbacks.
- **AppKit `NSPanel`** (not SwiftUI `Window`) — the overlay must be `.nonactivatingPanel`; SwiftUI windows always steal focus.
- **ONE `LauncherPanel` for the app's lifetime — never create a panel per show.** The v0.2–v0.3 pattern (fresh panel per hotkey toggle) gave WindowServer a new window identity seizing key on every toggle and is the prime suspect for the 2026-07-08 bug: after days of uptime, *other* focused apps (Slack, Dia) lost CSS hover/tooltips/cursor changes until Capture was killed. The panel is created once (`ensurePanel`), has `isReleasedWhenClosed = false`, is hidden with `orderOut` only, and is **never** `close()`d. Per-show freshness = `setContent(_:)` installing a **new `NSHostingView` + fresh `LauncherModel`** — a new hosting view is mandatory (not a `rootView` swap: same-type rootView replacement keeps SwiftUI structural identity, so `.onAppear` focus setup and `@FocusState` would not reset). `showPanel` resets to `seedHeight` (72) so a triage session's height never leaks into the next show.
- **`showPanel` ACTIVATES, then orders front** (2026-08, the Gyors fix): `NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps: true)` followed by `makeKeyAndOrderFront(nil)`. Under `.accessory` there is no Dock icon and no menu bar, so activating is invisible. This is the Spotlight / Alfred / Raycast / Gyors model.
  - **Why, and what it replaced:** until 2026-08 `showPanel` took key with `orderFrontRegardless()` + `makeKey()` and never activated. That leaves the previously-focused app *active* but with no key window anywhere in its process — and CSS hover, tooltips and cursor rects all hang off `NSTrackingArea` with `.activeInKeyWindow`, plus `mouseMoved` delivery requires key status. All three die together, in the foreground app, until Capture is killed. That is the 2026-07-08 bug's symptom exactly. Earlier suspects (per-toggle panel churn, the `frontmostApplication` hand-back) were both removed and the bug survived both.
  - **`hidePanel` is EXACTLY `orderOut(nil)` — nothing else.** No hand-back, no `makeFirstResponder(nil)`. Activation on show means `orderOut` is a normal deactivation and AppKit restores the previous app as both active *and* key on its own.
  - Still FORBIDDEN in the hide path: **`makeFirstResponder(nil)` before `orderOut`** (kills AppKit key-window return EVERY cycle — the v0.3.1 regression, 100% reproducible) and **`becomesKeyOnlyIfNeeded = true`** (makes key return flaky, 1 in 3). Panel keeps the NSPanel default (`false`).
  - This is a **multi-day soak bug** — per-cycle keyboard tests give false negatives (key return can work while hover return is broken). Verify by hovering Slack/Dia after days of uptime, not by toggling ten times.
- **Panel settings** (`Sources/LauncherPanel.swift`):

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## bear
Reading attachment file content (images, PDFs, other binaries) is not available through MCP tools on this server. Use the bearcli CLI:
  /Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli attachments save <note-id> --filename <name> > <file>
`/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli attachments save -h` covers usage. The CLI runs on the user's Mac and requires a shell with access to the user's filesystem. In clients whose shell runs in a sandbox, or that have no shell, attachment file content is not accessible — there is no MCP fallback for reading it.

Writing attachment file content has two paths. The `add_attachment_from_url` MCP tool fetches an HTTPS URL server-side; `http://`, `file://`, and `data:` are rejected. The bearcli CLI accepts bytes on stdin:
  cat <file> | /Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli attachments add <note-id> --filename <name>
`/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli attachments add -h` covers usage.

Both write paths insert a markdown link to the note. Bear renames on filename collision (e.g. `photo.jpg` → `photo 2.jpg`). The inserted link uses the resolved name. A follow-up edit adding the same file produces a duplicate.

External image links (`![](file:///…)` and `![](https://…)`) are not rendered by Bear. Writing one into a note produces nothing.

All other operations (note CRUD, search, tags, pins, listing and deleting attachments) use the MCP tools, not the CLI.

Addressing a section: an address is one or more heading lines joined by
newlines (write `\n`: the CLI interprets it, and JSON encodes it as a newline),
written as they appear, `#` markers and all (surrounding and repeated
spaces don't matter, but case does). A
heading that is unique in the note stands alone. If it
repeats, prepend one or more enclosing ancestor headings, ordered outer to
inner, and/or end with a 1-based index line that selects the Nth section
matching the lines above it, in document order. A trailing
`preamble` line addresses a section's lead text, above its first
subheading. Either pass a heading you know (a missing or ambiguous one
comes back with a helpful error suggesting addresses to retry with), or
outline the note to get every section's address. Examples:
  "## Install"               a uniquely-named section
  "# Setup\n## Install"      the ## Install under # Setup, when it repeats elsewhere
  "# Build\n## Install\n2"   the 2nd ## Install under # Build (ancestors and index combine)
  "## Install\npreamble"     the lead text of ## Install, above its first subheading

Bear notes use a CommonMark variant with these additions:
  ==highlight==, ~underline~, ~~strike~~
  ==🔴highlight== (or 🔵 🟢 🟡 🟣): colored highlight
  #tag, #multi word tag#, #nested/tag
  [[Note Title]] and [[Title|alias]] wikilinks
  $inline math$ and $$ ... $$ block math
  Tasks: - [ ] todo, - [x] done
  GFM-style tables (pipes required at both ends of every row)
  Callouts: > [!NOTE] (or TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION)
  YAML front matter: --- fenced, opening on the note's first line

A few CommonMark rules are also disabled: setext headings, indented
code blocks, and lazy continuation. Continuation lines in lists and
block quotes must carry their own indentation or > marker.

Bear soft-wraps long lines, so a paragraph hard-wrapped with
newlines shows as ragged short lines instead of reflowed text.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. ## claude.ai Omni
This MCP server provides tools for working with your Omni instance.

WORKFLOW:
1. If no modelId is configured via headers, call pickModel to see available models and select one, or leave modelId out of getData, askOmni, pickTopic, and listBranches: when the user can query exactly one model they use it, and otherwise they return the list to choose from. If it reports no models, skip the tools that take a modelId; the tools below that do not need one still work.
2. Choose the right tool for the question:
   - getData — a single, direct question answerable by one query (e.g. "how many users do I have?", "what was sales like last month?"). Returns the raw result set fast, in one call.
   - askOmni + checkStatus — an open-ended or multi-step question that needs planning, several queries, or a reasoned written answer. The agent can run multi-step analysis, build dashboards and reports, create visualizations and forecasts, and edit the semantic model (e.g. "analyze what's driving the revenue drop", "investigate churn last quarter", "build me a dashboard of signups by region", "add a revenue-per-user measure to the model"). askOmni starts the agent and returns a jobId immediately; then call checkStatus with that jobId to watch it work. The point of checkStatus is to narrate progress to the user, not just to detect completion: each call returns the agent's current step (and an 'instructions' field telling you what to relay), so tell the user what's happening whenever the step changes, then call checkStatus again — repeat until it returns the terminal result, which is where the synthesized answer comes back. Pass the conversationId from the result back into askOmni to ask a follow-up in the same thread. If the user asks you to stop a job, or says they no longer want its work, call cancelJob with its jobId — stopping your polling does not stop the job. Never cancel just because a job is slow, and tell the user what the result says actually happened. If the user says an answer was right or wrong, call submitFeedback with its jobId, their verdict, and their reason if they gave one.
3. Call the chosen tool with the modelId and prompt. If you do not pass a topic, getData will automatically pick an appropriate topic for the prompt.

You may optionally call pickTopic first if you want to choose a specific topic up front, but it is not required — getData and askOmni handle topic selection on their own when no topic is provided.

These tools let you retrieve real-time data from your connected databases by generating and executing queries from natural language prompts. This data is typically categorized as Business Intelligence or Analytical data in a tabular format. This gives your LLM the ability to answer questions about your specific business data, metrics, and analytics.

If a user provides SQL, study the SQL, describe what it is doing in plain english, and then call getData with the prompt as that plain english description of that SQL query.

When the query JSON is already in your context rather than a question, run it directly with runQuery — it skips query generation, so it spends no AI tokens and runs exactly the query you have.

The org's saved content is searchable: reach for searchContent before generating anything new when the user points at a dashboard they already have, then listDocumentQueries to see the queries it's built from. runSavedQuery then runs one of them and returns its current numbers, which beats generating a query for something they already have; when they want it narrowed (one customer, one id, another date range), pass runSavedQuery filters rather than regenerating the query. searchContent covers apps too, marking each hit with a 'type'; an identifier from a URL the user gives you works just as well. To read one yourself, getApp returns its full published HTML and settings, and getAppDraft returns the unpublished main-draft content when someone has edits in flight. If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),

    ))
  )

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## Field selection

All `find_*` and `get_*` tools support an optional `select` parameter — an array of field names.
When provided, only those fields are returned, reducing response size. `id` is always returned — including it in `select` is harmless but unnecessary.
Use this when you only need specific fields.
Include `_permissions` in `select` to see which actions you can perform on each record.
Only the fields in a tool's `select` enum can be projected. Some filters map to computed/virtual fields (e.g. `department`) that can be filtered on but are not stored on the record and cannot be selected.
Selecting a field and filtering on it are separate capabilities: you can only filter on the properties defined in a tool's `query` schema, which is often a smaller set than the selectable fields — a field you can `select` cannot necessarily be used as a query filter.

## Pagination

`find_*` tools return at most 20 records per page by default. To paginate, pass `$limit` and `$skip` inside the `query` object: `$limit` requests a different page size up to a hard cap of 2500, and `$skip` fetches subsequent pages by offset (set `$skip` to your current offset plus the previous `$limit`).

Every `find_*` response includes a `total` (the full match count) alongside the page of `data`. For "how many" / counting questions, read `total` — never fetch all records just to count them. Keep `$limit` small; only raise it when you genuinely need the rows themselves, and prefer a filtered query over a large page.

## Analysis

For grouped statistics, trends, joins, or calculations over many records, use `load_analysis_data` to copy permission-filtered pages from an available `find_*` tool into a snapshot, then `query_analysis_data` with read-only SQL. The source tool still requires its OAuth scope and your user permissions. Use the same optional `workspace` name on both tools to keep a conversation independent. Snapshots expire after one hour.

## claude.ai TheyDo

TheyDo is a journey management platform for understanding and improving customer experiences. This MCP surface is **read-only** — there are no tools to create, update, link, or delete resources. Use it to explore workspaces, summarise findings, and answer questions about journeys and the building blocks they reference.

## Tools at a glance

- **list_workspaces** — discover which workspaces the user has access to. Always call first when the workspace is not already known.
- **list** — browse a collection (paginated, supports search and saved views). Returns lightweight refs with a `path` for each item.
- **read** — fetch a single item or one of its linked relationships in full detail.
- **describe** — introspect a route to learn accepted query params, response fields, and which `_<link>.json` sub-paths exist. Use it whenever you are unsure of the schema rather than guessing.

## Terminology: Doc vs document

- **Doc** — a rich-text artifact (report, summary, brief) authored inside TheyDo. Lives under `/documents/{id}.md` and is referred to with `entity_type="DOCUMENT"`. Always call these "Docs" in your replies to the user.
- **document** (lowercase) — raw source material such as interview transcripts, surveys, or CSV files. These are surfaced as Data Sources (under `/data-sources/`), not as Docs. Never refer to a Doc as a "document" in your replies.

The path `/documents/` and the literal `DOCUMENT` are API contracts and keep those names — the distinction is only about what you say to the user.

## Terminology: "insights", "evidence", "data", "learnings"

In TheyDo, **Insight** is a specific building block (`/insights/` — bite-sized interpreted customer knowledge, typed Pain/Gain/Need/Observation). But when users say "insights", "evidence", "data", "learnings", "findings", or "research", they often mean the broader evidence in the platform, not just that one collection:

- **Data Sources** (`/data-sources/`) — raw research material: transcripts, surveys, CSVs.
- **Quotes** (`/quotes/`) — verbatim customer statements extracted from data sources.
- **Insights** (`/insights/`) — interpreted conclusions backed by quotes.
- Sometimes also **Docs**, **Metrics** (quantitative evidence), or **Opportunities** derived from the above.

Do not silently equate these words with the `/insights/` collection. When the request is ambiguous ("what insights do we have about onboarding?", "show me the evidence", "what does the data say?"), either ask one clarifying question, or cover the evidence stack — search `/insights/`, `/quotes/`, and `/data-sources/` — and state in your reply which TheyDo objects each result came from. Reserve the bare word "Insight" in replies for the building block, and use "evidence" or "source material" when referring to quotes and data sources.

## Domain model

### Journeys

A journey is a series of steps, designed from the customer's perspective, that contextualises qualitative and quantitative data. It has two dimensions:

- **Horizontal axis (customer timeline)**: Phases group Steps. Steps reveal what a customer sees, does, thinks, and feels.
- **Vertical axis (business context)**: Lanes map building blocks to the relevant steps. Each building-block type gets its own lane. A single block can span multiple steps.

**Visibility.** `read /journeys/{id}.json` reflects the user's *current view configuration*. Phases, steps, and lanes hidden in the user's view are omitted, along with any building blocks whose only placements were on hidden cells. The response is authoritative: do not reference phases, steps, lanes, or building blocks that are not in it. Trust the latest read over earlier conversation turns — prior turns may mention items that have since been hidden.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Granola__search_transcripts
definition.description:
Find specific words or quotes in accessible meeting transcripts in the active workspace. Returns ranked passages with approximate timestamps.

Supply meeting_ids when known, batching meetings that share the same terms and filters. Matching is literal; put alternative words in one keywords array, e.g. ["pricing", "price", "cost"]. For what a person or company said, use participant (names/companies) or attendee_emails/attendee_domains (invite list). participant is an AND filter on metadata that can be incomplete, so for broader questions also search their name and the topic in keywords without it.

Known meetings with no indexed match are also searched in their current transcripts. Without meeting_ids, search relies on an asynchronously updated index and groups duplicate recordings; empty results do not prove a topic was never discussed.

Follow next_cursor even on empty pages, passing only cursor and optionally limit. If completion_status is incomplete, narrow the search or read known transcripts.

Read surrounding dialogue with get_meeting_transcript using meeting_id, the passage's chunk_ids and transcript_version; adjacent chunk IDs continue, and omitting chunk_ids reads the whole conversation.

counts is cumulative across pages; total_matching_chunks is a first-page estimate, null for direct search. Neither counts spoken mentions.

Use another tool when:
- The term is likely in the notes, or the user wants meetings about a topic: use search_meetings
- You need the whole conversation: use get_meeting_transcript

keywords.description: Required for a new search. Entries are alternatives (OR); all words within an entry must occur in one chunk, in any order. Accepts an array or comma-separated string.

meeting_ids.description: Restrict to these meetings (UUIDs or public note IDs, max 100). Batch IDs sharing the same terms and filters. Omit to search all accessible indexed meetings.

items.description: Meeting UUID, public note ID (not_...) or Granola note link

cursor.description: Pass next_cursor from a previous result; only limit may accompany it. Omit or pass an empty string for the first page. Cursors expire after 15 minutes.

limit.description: Passages per page with meeting_ids; otherwise meetings per page. Default 10, capped at 20.

from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. Dates and offsetless times use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable).

to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable). Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

participant.description: Filter by participant name, email, company name, or domain in meeting participant metadata. Combines with keywords, dates, meeting_ids, attendee_emails, and attendee_domains using AND. Mentions in the transcript alone do not match. Missing participant metadata can hide relevant meetings; metadata does not prove attendance.

attendee_emails.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes any of these emails, e.g. ["alice@acme.com"]

attendee_domains.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes anyone at these email domains, including subdomains, e.g. ["acme.com"]

Welsani is a wealth-management vault: investments owned by entities (people, companies, households), the documents behind them, the money that flows (cashflow, bank accounts), insurance policies and the action items that follow from all of it.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Granola__search_transcripts
definition.description:
Find specific words or quotes in accessible meeting transcripts in the active workspace. Returns ranked passages with approximate timestamps.

Supply meeting_ids when known, batching meetings that share the same terms and filters. Matching is literal; put alternative words in one keywords array, e.g. ["pricing", "price", "cost"]. For what a person or company said, use participant (names/companies) or attendee_emails/attendee_domains (invite list). participant is an AND filter on metadata that can be incomplete, so for broader questions also search their name and the topic in keywords without it.

Known meetings with no indexed match are also searched in their current transcripts. Without meeting_ids, search relies on an asynchronously updated index and groups duplicate recordings; empty results do not prove a topic was never discussed.

Follow next_cursor even on empty pages, passing only cursor and optionally limit. If completion_status is incomplete, narrow the search or read known transcripts.

Read surrounding dialogue with get_meeting_transcript using meeting_id, the passage's chunk_ids and transcript_version; adjacent chunk IDs continue, and omitting chunk_ids reads the whole conversation.

counts is cumulative across pages; total_matching_chunks is a first-page estimate, null for direct search. Neither counts spoken mentions.

Use another tool when:
- The term is likely in the notes, or the user wants meetings about a topic: use search_meetings
- You need the whole conversation: use get_meeting_transcript

keywords.description: Required for a new search. Entries are alternatives (OR); all words within an entry must occur in one chunk, in any order. Accepts an array or comma-separated string.

meeting_ids.description: Restrict to these meetings (UUIDs or public note IDs, max 100). Batch IDs sharing the same terms and filters. Omit to search all accessible indexed meetings.

items.description: Meeting UUID, public note ID (not_...) or Granola note link

cursor.description: Pass next_cursor from a previous result; only limit may accompany it. Omit or pass an empty string for the first page. Cursors expire after 15 minutes.

limit.description: Passages per page with meeting_ids; otherwise meetings per page. Default 10, capped at 20.

from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. Dates and offsetless times use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable).

to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable). Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

participant.description: Filter by participant name, email, company name, or domain in meeting participant metadata. Combines with keywords, dates, meeting_ids, attendee_emails, and attendee_domains using AND. Mentions in the transcript alone do not match. Missing participant metadata can hide relevant meetings; metadata does not prove attendance.

attendee_emails.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes any of these emails, e.g. ["alice@acme.com"]

attendee_domains.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes anyone at these email domains, including subdomains, e.g. ["acme.com"]

content.thinking:
I'm sorting out the note's formats: top-level bullets under `## Captures` that may carry a timestamp prefix, with indented continuation lines, plus checkboxes under `## Q4` and some plain bullets. I'm weighing whether list items should be limited to the Captures section or picked up from anywhere in the note, since Goals sits outside it.

I'm weighing whether to parse top-level bullets across the whole note or only under `## Captures`, and I'm leaning toward the whole note with each item's indented children. Goals' checkboxes would get included, which seems harmless since the user picks the list. Each item's display text drops the `- ` marker and any timestamp prefix, while the original datetime is kept for filing. The list actions are settled: Enter on the pinned row keeps the item in place, Enter on a destination files it there under its original timestamp, ⌘⌫ discards it, and Tab skips. I still need to decide how moving works.

I'm settling how the source picker should work: the Inbox would be the first row, followed by the lists. Destinations in list mode will exclude the list being processed, so nothing gets filed back into itself. Items from a list will be taken in document order, top to bottom.

I'm settling on the source picker, with the Inbox as the first row and the lists below it, so Enter on the Inbox still works the same way. That adds one keystroke to the Inbox path, which I'll note. Removing a list item needs an exact match on its raw block, so I'm working out how to do that reliably.

I'm working out how to remove a list item cleanly, since the generic remover would eat the blank line before the `#list` tag. I'll write a dedicated line-based remover that takes the item's block along with one trailing newline.

I'm checking how list items get removed, since a generic remover could eat the blank line before the `#list` tag. I'm also weighing whether `InboxEntry` can be reused for list items or needs its own shape.

I'm weighing whether to rename `InboxEntry` to a more general `TriageEntry` that carries an explicit optional `datetime`, so list items and inbox entries can share the same shape. The parser would fill in the datetime from the header, and I'd check whether `header` is used anywhere else before dropping it.

content.content:
Single-purpose macOS overlay launcher for Charles's Bear-based second brain. Press a global hotkey, a flat themed bar opens, type a thought, hit Enter — then a destination picker filters projects/people/personal areas as you type. Enter on the pinned Inbox row (or with nothing typed) sends the capture to the pinned Bear "Inbox" note; Enter on a destination files it **immediately**, verbatim, into that note. A second hotkey opens Process Inbox: Tinder-style triage of existing inbox items.

```
capture:  ⏎ text → picker → ⏎ dest ──BearCLI casEdit──▶ dest note's section (see below)
                          → ⏎ inbox ──BearCLI casEdit──▶ Inbox note (prepend under H1)
triage:   entry prefilled (editable) → picker → ⏎ dest    same, under the entry's ORIGINAL timestamp, + remove block
                                              → ⏎ inbox   keep it in the Inbox and move on (same as ⇥)
                                              → ⌘⌫        remove block only  ·  ⇥ skip  ·  esc exit
any bearcli failure ─▶ DailyCapture.send(text, marker:) → Inbox via x-callback + notification
```
- **Ranking**: title-prefix 100 > word-boundary 80 > fuzzy subsequence 40+compactness, plus recency `20·exp(−ageDays/14)` and MRU `15·exp(−idx/5)` keyed by note id. Empty query = top rows by recency+MRU with Inbox pinned at row 0, so ⏎⏎ means "straight to inbox" (capture) or "keep it there" (triage).
Credentials stay in your macOS Keychain. An unused connection expires after 30 days; sign in again from Settings.

## Process Inbox

`⌃⌘⇧Space` (or the menu item) triages existing inbox entries oldest-first, one at a time — prefilled and editable, with a `4/31` counter:

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| `Enter` → type + `Enter` | File to the matched destination and remove from the Inbox |
| `Enter` → `Enter` (empty) | Keep it in the Inbox and move on |
| `⌘⌫` | Discard (remove from the Inbox) |
| `Tab` | Skip (leave in the Inbox) |
| `Esc` | Exit |

Every decision advances instantly; the Bear writes happen behind it.

## Configuration

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build a Release configuration of Capture and zip the .app bundle for GitHub Releases.
#
# Usage: scripts/release.sh 0.1.0
#
# Output: dist/Capture-v<VERSION>.zip
#
# Upload to a GitHub Release with:
#   gh release create v<VERSION> dist/Capture-v<VERSION>.zip --title "Capture v<VERSION>"

set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <version>" >&2
  echo "Example: $0 0.1.0" >&2
  exit 1
fi

VERSION="$1"

command -v xcodegen  >/dev/null || { echo "xcodegen not found. brew install xcodegen" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v xcodebuild >/dev/null || { echo "xcodebuild not found. Install Xcode." >&2; exit 1; }

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

rm -rf build dist
mkdir -p dist

xcodegen generate

xcodebuild \
  -project Capture.xcodeproj \
  -scheme Capture \
  -configuration Release \
  -derivedDataPath build \
  ARCHS="arm64 x86_64" \
  ONLY_ACTIVE_ARCH=NO \
  MARKETING_VERSION="$VERSION" \
  CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION="$VERSION" \
  clean build

APP_PATH="build/Build/Products/Release/Capture.app"
if [[ ! -d "$APP_PATH" ]]; then
  echo "Build succeeded but $APP_PATH not found" >&2
  exit 1
fi

ZIP_PATH="dist/Capture-v${VERSION}.zip"
ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc --keepParent "$APP_PATH" "$ZIP_PATH"

echo
echo "Built: $ZIP_PATH"
echo
echo "Next:"
echo "  gh release create v${VERSION} ${ZIP_PATH} --title \"Capture v${VERSION}\""

# Capture — agent notes

## What this is

Single-purpose macOS overlay launcher for Charles's Bear-based second brain. Press a global hotkey, a flat themed bar opens, type a thought, hit Enter — then a destination picker filters projects/people/personal areas as you type. Enter on the pinned Inbox row (or with nothing typed) sends the capture to the pinned Bear "Inbox" note; Enter on a destination files it **immediately**, verbatim, into that note. A second hotkey opens Process Inbox: pick the Inbox or a `#list` note, then Tinder-style triage of its items.

The point is **speed**: hotkey → bar → Enter → gone. Lives entirely as a menu-bar app. No history, no plugins, no main window, no Dock icon. The bar persists when focus is lost — only Esc / Enter / the hotkey itself hide it. Multi-line capture grows the bar downward up to 5 lines, then scrolls internally.

## Design principles (Charles's explicit choices — don't violate)

1. **Speed is the product.** Every keystroke-to-paint under 300ms; in practice <1ms because the keystroke path never does I/O. Destinations live in memory (refreshed async at launch, on every panel show, and via the Refresh Projects menu item). All Bear writes are optimistic: the panel hides / triage advances instantly, work happens behind it.
2. **bearcli for everything.** All Bear I/O goes through the `BearCLI` actor wrapping `/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli` (ships inside Bear 2.8+, works headless). Writes only via CAS: `cat --format json` (returns `content` + `hash`) → transform → `overwrite --base <hash>`; a concurrent Bear.app change rejects the write (exit 1, "Note has changed since last read") and we re-read and retry ×3. **A whole-note `cat` is the only source of the hash.** It used to be `show --fields hash,content`; bearcli 2.9.x dropped `hash` from `show`'s field set, which broke every read with "Unknown field: hash" — triage closed instantly and captures silently took the fallback path (2026-08-23). Re-check this if bearcli is upgraded. **Never write Bear's SQLite directly.** The x-callback URI template survives only as the fallback path.
3. **No daemons, no background agents.** No queues, no Redis, no background workers, no launchd. Charles explicitly rejected daemon infra — don't reintroduce it. The per-capture `claude -p` filing agent was removed on 2026-10-13: the second brain's rule is that nothing writes to Bear in the background.
4. **A capture is never lost.** Every failure path degrades to an Inbox write via the fallback URI template with a backtick-wrapped `` → `#tag` `` marker (backticks so Bear doesn't tag the Inbox note) plus a notification. The triage parser skips marker-carrying blocks.
5. **Human decides, verbatim lands.** The picker is Charles's routing decision. A capture lands exactly as typed and stays where it lands; turning captures into notes is his job.
6. **Themed minimal UI, modelled on [Gyors](https://github.com/balintb/Gyors)** (2026-08 restyle; its macOS layer is SwiftUI over an `NSPanel`, so its numbers port directly). **Ember default** — Gyors' published theme, verbatim: bg `#120C10`, accent `#F97316`, text `#FBF3EC`/`#A89B91`/`#6B5E54`, backgroundOpacity 0.88. Eleven themes in Settings (`Theme.swift`, one struct literal each: Ember, Solarized Light/Dark, Gruvbox Light/Dark, Catppuccin Latte/Mocha, Nord, Dracula, Tokyo Night, Mono Dark).
   - **Three text tiers**: `foreground` (primary) / `secondary` (banner, status — real content) / `dim` (hints, placeholders, ms readout). **Never bake `.opacity()` into a text colour** — over the blur substrate the alpha multiplies and the text goes mushy. Use a solid hex. Alpha on `selectionBackground` is fine; it's a background.
   - **Translucency**: `NSVisualEffectView` (`.popover`, `.behindWindow`, `.active`) as a sibling of the hosting view; per-theme `usesBlur` + `backgroundOpacity`. Charles declined Raycast's glass in 2026-07 but chose Gyors' in 2026-08.
   - **Geometry**: 720 wide, cornerRadius 14 (was 16), 20pt gutter everywhere so the leaf name lines up under the typed text, 36pt rows, no border, instant show/hide, no row icons, no footer bar, no `>` prompt glyph.
   - **Type**: SF Pro throughout (Charles found a pixel font "too much"). Both inputs 22pt `.light`; leaf name 14pt `.medium`; banner 13; chip 11 semibold; hints and ms readout 11.
   - **Selection**: flat full-bleed `accent × selectionOpacity` across the whole row, radius 0, no inset (replaced 2026-07's inset rounded highlight).
   - **`Divider().opacity(0.3)`** full-bleed between the query row and the list.
   - **TheyDo chips** right-aligned per row (2026-07, replaced rainbow badges Charles disliked): one shared hue set `Theme.theydoKinds` (violet/pink/teal/amber/blue/ink-gray/orange for lists/grape for agendas), a pastel **gradient** fill + same-hue tinted text via `Theme.chip(for:)`, derived against each theme's background/foreground so chips adapt to light/dark. `kindColors` stays per-theme-overridable (Mono Dark overrides to stay monochrome).
   - Fixed-height 8-row **scrollable** viewport (empty query lists *all* destinations; the panel never resizes while filtering — only on stage transitions).
   - Placeholder text must be explicitly themed via `prompt: Text(...).foregroundColor(theme.secondary)` — default placeholders ignore the theme and vanish on dark themes. `secondary`, not `dim`: `dim` is the tertiary tone and reads too dark for a placeholder (Charles, 2026-08-21).

## Project layout

```
project.yml                 XcodeGen spec — single source of truth for the Xcode project
Sources/
  CaptureApp.swift          @main App + MenuBarExtra (Open/Process Inbox/Refresh) + Settings scene
  AppDelegate.swift         .accessory policy, both hotkeys, panel lifecycle, --show-on-launch dev flag
  LauncherPanel.swift       NSPanel subclass (non-activating, transparent, blur sibling, children clipped)
  LauncherView.swift        Stage-driven SwiftUI view: compose / route / loading / done
  LauncherModel.swift       @Observable stage machine (capture + triage modes, all transitions)

  - `backgroundColor = .clear`, `isOpaque = false`, `animationBehavior = .none`.
  - **Rounding lives on the children, never the container.** `cornerRadius` + `masksToBounds` together force offscreen rasterisation, and on macOS 26 that buffer composites *opaque*. - **Focus swaps between stages need `DispatchQueue.main.async`** — the target TextField is created in the same transaction as the stage change.
- **One runtime dependency**: [`KeyboardShortcuts`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/KeyboardShortcuts) (global hotkeys). Declared in `project.yml`'s `packages:`.
- **`NSWorkspace.open` with `config.activates = false`** on the fallback path so Bear never steals focus.

## Hotkeys

`⌃⌘Space` capture, `⌃⌘⇧Space` process inbox — both rebindable via `KeyboardShortcuts.Recorder` rows in Settings (persisted in UserDefaults; the `default:` in `HotkeyName.swift` only affects fresh installs).

## The Inbox note

Pinned Bear note, id `E01000CB-BE7D-4FCB-8340-BBE23A4569B9` (configurable in Settings). Blocks are `**yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm**\ntext`, newest on top, blank-line separated; the note ends with the `#inbox` tag line. `InboxParser` tolerates date-only headers and empty bodies, and skips blocks whose header contains `→` (fallback-parked). The note must stay unencrypted.

## Distribution

Personal use, ad-hoc signed. `scripts/release.sh <version>` produces a zipped `.app` for a GitHub Release. Gatekeeper prompts once: right-click → Open, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Capture.app`.

The bar persists when focus is lost — only Esc / Enter / the hotkey itself hide it. Multi-line capture grows the bar downward up to 5 lines, then scrolls internally.

## Design principles (Charles's explicit choices — don't violate)

1. **Speed is the product.** Every keystroke-to-paint under 300ms; in practice <1ms because the keystroke path never does I/O. Destinations live in memory (refreshed async at launch, on every panel show, and via the Refresh Projects menu item). All Bear writes are optimistic: the panel hides / triage advances instantly, work happens behind it.
2. **bearcli for everything.** All Bear I/O goes through the `BearCLI` actor wrapping `/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli` (ships inside Bear 2.8+, works headless). Writes only via CAS: `cat --format json` (returns `content` + `hash`) → transform → `overwrite --base <hash>`; a concurrent Bear.app change rejects the write (exit 1, "Note has changed since last read") and we re-read and retry ×3. **A whole-note `cat` is the only source of the hash.** It used to be `show --fields hash,content`; bearcli 2.9.x dropped `hash` from `show`'s field set, which broke every read with "Unknown field: hash" — triage closed instantly and captures silently took the fallback path (2026-08-23). 3. **No daemons, no background agents.** No queues, no Redis, no background workers, no launchd. Charles explicitly rejected daemon infra — don't reintroduce it. # Capture — agent notes

## What this is

Single-purpose macOS overlay launcher for Charles's Bear-based second brain. Press a global hotkey, a flat themed bar opens, type a thought, hit Enter — then a destination picker filters projects/people/personal areas as you type. Enter on the pinned Inbox row (or with nothing typed) sends the capture to the pinned Bear "Inbox" note; Enter on a destination files it **immediately**, verbatim, into that note. A second hotkey opens Process Inbox: pick the Inbox or a `#list` note, then Tinder-style triage of its items.

The point is **speed**: hotkey → bar → Enter → gone. Lives entirely as a menu-bar app. No history, no plugins, no main window, no Dock icon. The bar persists when focus is lost — only Esc / Enter / the hotkey itself hide it. Multi-line capture grows the bar downward up to 5 lines, then scrolls internally.

## Design principles (Charles's explicit choices — don't violate)

1. **Speed is the product.** Every keystroke-to-paint under 300ms; in practice <1ms because the keystroke path never does I/O. Destinations live in memory (refreshed async at launch, on every panel show, and via the Refresh Projects menu item). All Bear writes are optimistic: the panel hides / triage advances instantly, work happens behind it.
2. **bearcli for everything.** All Bear I/O goes through the `BearCLI` actor wrapping `/Applications/Bear.app/Contents/MacOS/bearcli` (ships inside Bear 2.8+, works headless). Writes only via CAS: `cat --format json` (returns `content` + `hash`) → transform → `overwrite --base <hash>`; a concurrent Bear.app change rejects the write (exit 1, "Note has changed since last read") and we re-read and retry ×3. **A whole-note `cat` is the only source of the hash.** It used to be `show --fields hash,content`; bearcli 2.9.x dropped `hash` from `show`'s field set, which broke every read with "Unknown field: hash" — triage closed instantly and captures silently took the fallback path (2026-08-23). Re-check this if bearcli is upgraded. **Never write Bear's SQLite directly.** The x-callback URI template survives only as the fallback path.
3. **No daemons, no background agents.** No queues, no Redis, no background workers, no launchd. Charles explicitly rejected daemon infra — don't reintroduce it. The per-capture `claude -p` filing agent was removed on 2026-10-13: the second brain's rule is that nothing writes to Bear in the background.
4. **A capture is never lost.** Every failure path degrades to an Inbox write via the fallback URI template with a backtick-wrapped `` → `#tag` `` marker (backticks so Bear doesn't tag the Inbox note) plus a notification. The triage parser skips marker-carrying blocks.
5. **Human decides, verbatim lands.** The picker is Charles's routing decision. A capture lands exactly as typed and stays where it lands; turning captures into notes is his job.
